points.heading: Simple tenses
points.body:
In the indicative mood we present facts as real. Five simple tenses locate the action without a perfect auxiliary: present, imperfect (past progressive / used-to sense), preterite (simple past), future, and simple conditional. Each tense changes form while keeping the verb’s core meaning.

Why it matters: without these five clear, compound (perfect) forms get confusing. Present names habits or what is happening now (I sing / I am singing). Imperfect paints background, habit, or ongoing past (I was singing / I used to sing). Preterite marks a finished past event (I sang). Future places what has not yet happened (I will sing). Conditional expresses hypothesis, politeness, or a possible result (I would sing).

Worked examples with sing (I): I sing, I was singing, I sang, I will sing, I would sing. With live (we): we live, we were living / we used to live, we lived, we will live, we would live. Notice how imperfect does not «close» the action while simple past does.

Practice tip: conjugate one regular verb in first-person singular through all five. Then write five minimal sentences, changing the time frame: today / as a child / yesterday / tomorrow / if I could.

Common mistake: using progressive/used-to when you mean a finished plot event («Yesterday I was going to the cinema» if you mean you went → «Yesterday I went»). Another: mixing simple past and present perfect without a reason.

points.heading: Compound tenses
points.body:
The five compound (perfect) tenses use an auxiliary + past participle. English mainly uses have / had / will have / would have + participle (eaten, written, said). The participle stays fixed; only the auxiliary changes for time and person.

Why it matters: perfect aspect shows the action as «already done» relative to a time anchor. Present perfect (I have sung) links past action to present relevance. Pluperfect (I had sung) is a past before another past. Anterior preterite is rare/literary. Future perfect (I will have sung) projects completion by a future point. Conditional perfect (I would have sung) marks what would have happened in a past hypothesis.

Examples. «I have left three times this week» (present perfect). «When I arrived, she had already left» (pluperfect). «We will have finished by five» (future perfect). «I would have come if you had called» (conditional perfect).

Practice tip: write have / had / will have / would have + the same participle (eaten or written). Mark auxiliary vs participle. Memorize three irregular participles you use often (written, said, done).

Common mistake: inventing regular participles for irregular verbs («writed», «goed»). Another: changing the participle as if it were a finite verb («we have ates»).

points.heading: Usage: simple vs compound
points.body:
Choose simple or compound by relative time and aspect. Labels are not enough: ask what temporal relation you want to express.

Practical guide. A closed past moment («Yesterday I finished») → simple past. A result still relevant («I have already finished») → present perfect. Past habit or background → imperfect / used to / past progressive. Present hypothesis → conditional. Already done before another past → pluperfect.

Contrasted examples. «I finished the book yesterday» (closed). «I have finished the book» (result still matters). «I was reading when the phone rang» (background + event). «I had read the chapter before class» (pluperfect).

Practice tip: for each idea, choose the tense and justify in one sentence («I use simple past because…»). Rewrite five short sentences changing only the tense and explain what nuance shifts.

Common mistake: present perfect with a finished yesterday-anchor in careful style («Yesterday I have gone» → prefer «Yesterday I went»). Another: progressive for a single completed plot beat when simple past is clearer.

lesson.summary: Master the ten indicative tenses: five simple (present, imperfect, preterite, future, conditional) and five compound with auxiliary + participle, knowing when to choose each.
